channel.title: testD — Sexual health & harm reduction articles
channel.description: New articles from testD on HIV, PrEP, PEP, STIs and harm reduction.

item.title: HIV and STI Home Test Kits in Thailand: 5 Types and How to Choose
item.description: Finger-prick HIV, oral HIV, syphilis, dual HIV & syphilis, and gonorrhea & chlamydia kits: what each detects, window periods, and what to do after your result.

item.title: Choosing a finger-prick kit with a safe sharps-disposal plan
item.description: Before buying a finger-prick kit, plan secure sharps containment and an accepted local disposal route—not just the testing session.

item.title: Pregnancy and planning a family: kits do not replace antenatal care
item.description: Self-testing can start a conversation, but pregnancy care requires coordinated screening, interpretation, and treatment that kits cannot provide.

item.title: Gonorrhea/chlamydia kits: why the sample site matters
item.description: Choose gonorrhea/chlamydia testing around exposed body sites and the exact specimen accepted—not a claim that one kit checks everything.

item.title: HIV and syphilis kits do not screen for every STI
item.description: HIV and syphilis results do not describe your entire sexual health. Other infections and exposure sites may require different tests.

item.title: Syphilis kits and RPR/VDRL: different questions, different tests
item.description: Treponemal tests and RPR/VDRL play different roles, especially after past treatment. A retail screening result cannot determine treatment needs by itself.

item.title: A negative result: planning repeat testing around exposure
item.description: Plan repeat testing from exposure dates, the actual test used, and antiretroviral use—not simply from how many kits remain.

item.title: Reactive results: why buying more brands is not confirmation
item.description: A reactive screening result calls for clinical follow-up, not a majority vote across brands. Different results do not cancel one another out.

item.title: An invalid result: what to check before buying a replacement
item.description: An invalid test has not answered your infection question. Review the instructions and kit condition before choosing another self-test or clinic testing.

item.title: Travelling with test kits: choosing and protecting your supplies
item.description: Plan around the kit’s labeled storage conditions, your route, and access to care—not just whether the box fits in your luggage.

item.title: Buying kits for a partner or friend: consent before a bulk order
item.description: Before buying a kit for someone else, agree on consent, privacy, and support without making testing or result-sharing a condition of trust.

item.title: Free HIV kits or buying online: choosing the right route
item.description: Compare urgency, access requirements, privacy, and follow-up. Neither a free offer nor a paid purchase establishes test quality by itself.

item.title: Questions to ask a seller before ordering an HIV/STI kit
item.description: Ask about exact identity, permitted users, assay purpose, and support. Product information from a seller cannot replace an individualized clinical assessment.

item.title: Cheap or expensive kits: compare without equating price with quality
item.description: Price may reflect packaging, accessories, or service—not test performance. Compare authorization, suitability, and total practical costs instead.

item.title: Before buying: plan a private space and a result-reading routine
item.description: Plan privacy, lighting, timing, and follow-up before ordering. A private home test still needs a workable routine and a safe route to support.

item.title: Thai and English instructions: choose a kit you understand
item.description: Choose instructions you understand that match the exact product, including warnings, sample requirements, result timing, and interpretation—not just a translated sales page.

item.title: Small print and fiddly steps: choosing an accessible test kit
item.description: Assess whether you can read, handle, time, and interpret a kit before buying. “Easy to use” is not a substitute for accessible instructions.

item.title: Fear of needles: choosing an HIV testing option without pressure
item.description: Needle fear does not make testing impossible. Consider authorized alternatives, supportive services, and the timing of a possible exposure without pressuring yourself.

item.title: Checking included accessories before choosing a finger-prick kit
item.description: Check the exact kit’s contents list, separately required items, and sharps-disposal needs instead of assuming every finger-prick kit includes the same accessories.

item.title: A hot or damaged test-kit parcel: deciding whether to use it
item.description: A warm parcel alone cannot establish damage. Check the product limits, protective packaging, and available evidence before deciding whether to use it.

item.title: Expiry and storage: checking a kit before paying
item.description: Check expiry, storage requirements, and product identity before buying. A clean-looking box does not establish that a kit remains suitable for use.

item.title: Possible syphilis symptoms: a kit purchase or a clinic visit?
item.description: A suspicious sore or rash calls for clinical assessment without waiting for a kit, because a negative screen cannot explain symptoms.

item.title: Previously treated syphilis: what a home kit cannot tell you
item.description: Treponemal reactivity can persist after treatment; follow-up relies on clinical history and appropriately interpreted RPR/VDRL results.

item.title: After PEP: choose testing around clinical follow-up
item.description: After PEP, testing should follow your medication history and clinical plan—not a retail promise of a final answer.

item.title: Choosing a kit while taking PrEP: keep clinic monitoring
item.description: A self-test should not replace PrEP follow-up because antiretrovirals can affect detection and result interpretation.

item.title: Recent exposure: what buying a kit today can and cannot answer
item.description: A test today may provide baseline information, but it cannot immediately exclude infection from a recent exposure.

item.title: Dual HIV/syphilis or separate kits: what to compare
item.description: Compare targets, intended use, and separate result meanings—not just how many infections appear on the box.

item.title: Self-test versus professional-use kits: why the label matters
item.description: Similar-looking devices are not interchangeable: the intended-user label matters before testing at home.

item.title: Before buying a test kit online: checking labels and authorization
item.description: Match the exact product and permitted use to official information rather than trusting badges, reviews, or seller claims.

item.title: Oral fluid or finger-prick: choosing the sample you can handle
item.description: Compare sample handling and comfort without assuming that specimen type reveals test generation or suitability after exposure.

item.title: Choosing your first HIV and syphilis kit: a decision checklist
item.description: Start with your reason for testing, exposure timing, and follow-up options—not a brand or advertising claim.

item.title: Where can I get free PrEP in Thailand? Check eligibility and book with SWING
item.description: Find out how to check PrEP eligibility and costs, prepare for a consultation, and book SWING through testD without assuming every visit is free for everyone.

item.title: When is an HIV test reliable? Understanding 14, 30, 45 and 90 days
item.description: HIV testing windows depend on the test: compare antibody tests, laboratory antigen/antibody tests and NAT, and learn when negative results need repeat testing.

item.title: Faint line on an HIV self-test: what it means and what to do next
item.description: Read a faint HIV self-test line using the specific kit instructions. Learn the difference between reactive, negative and invalid results, and when to seek confirmatory testing.
